projects.title: Imitation Learning Tool
projects.subtitle: Custom PCB, firmware, and UI for a robot-arm training data collection tool
projects.description: Designed a ROS-enabled RP2040 controller from scratch across three PCB revisions. Now used in production to collect imitation learning data.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Nupeak Robotics needed a handheld tool to record human demonstrations for training robot arms. Over a three-month internship after my freshman year I designed the board, firmware, and UI from scratch, with no prior embedded systems experience. It now ships internally as the company's imitation learning data collection device.

sections.heading: The Challenge
sections.content: Design review with the CTO surfaced four problems with V1 that had to be solved without growing the board or slipping the timeline:
bullets: Signal integrity issues risking dropped comms between the MCU and peripherals
EMI from the motor driver threatening sensor accuracy
Tight space for component placement and routing
Losses on the stepped-down 12V → 5V / 3.3V power rails

sections.heading: Three Revisions
bullets: V1: first board from scratch in KiCad, RP2040, BLDC motor controller, TFT display, tactile buttons
V2: smaller footprint, motor return paths separated from sensitive nets, widened power rails, 4-layer SGPS stackup, nothing routed under the USB differential pair
V3: buck converter to cover the BLDC power budget, solder jumpers to reassign GPIO without a respin, haptics (LRA + driver), signals confined to outer layers

images.caption: V2: refined routing and smaller footprint
V3: buck converter, solder jumpers, haptics

sections.heading: Firmware & UI
bullets: Core 0: ROS Serial layer with custom service/client nodes exposing actuators and sensors to ROS Noetic
Core 1: LVGL TFT interface built in SquareLine Studio for live status and control
Splitting the cores keeps latency-sensitive I/O from ever blocking the render loop

images.caption: V2 UI: battery, tracking status, and recording count over ROS
Integrated into the imitation learning platform

projects.title: System-on-Module
projects.subtitle: Compact RP2350B module for local joint control on a quadruped
projects.description: Stackable castellated module that puts a controller next to each actuator. Four revisions to keep signals clean amid twelve motors of PWM noise.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Each joint on our quadruped needed its own local controller so the main processor wasn't handling every motor command. I designed a deliberately minimal RP2350B module (MCU, crystal, flash, nothing else) that stacks onto the main board through castellated edges and sits right next to the actuator.

sections.heading: The Challenge
bullets: Twelve motors switching at high frequency, all coupling noise into everything nearby
Module has to fit the tight space next to each joint
High-speed inter-module comms that can't drop data
Mechanical team needed castellated edges for board-to-board stacking

sections.heading: Approach
bullets: Length-matched, impedance-controlled differential pairs, since small timing skew means corrupted data
Stitching vias throughout for clean return paths and lower EMI
Separate power and ground planes so digital noise stays off sensitive nets
Custom castellated footprint in V2, since no stock footprint fit our stacking scheme
Power regulation and motor drivers stay on the carrier board, keeping the module simple

images.caption: V2: castellated edges for board-to-board stacking
V3: custom castellated footprint, optimized signal integrity

projects.title: D-Stock Racing Telemetry System
projects.subtitle: Cockpit and telemetry boards for a high-speed electric race boat
projects.description: Led cockpit board design in Altium: rigid-flex PCB, 48V to 3.3V power tree, full HV/LV isolation. Three revisions to survive vibration, water, and motor noise.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: I led the cockpit board through three revisions and contributed to the GPS/CAN telemetry board for D-Stock boat racing. The final cockpit board is a rigid-flex design with complete HV/LV galvanic isolation, 40% smaller than the version before it, with two connector failure points designed out entirely.

sections.heading: The Challenge
bullets: Constant vibration and water exposure, where connectors were the obvious weak point
A 48V motor bus sharing a board with 3.3V logic, with no ground loops
GPS and CAN signals routed through a very electrically noisy environment

sections.heading: Three Revisions
bullets: V1: two-layer board, M12 marine connectors, DPDT relay for HV contactor control, SD card logging, basic HV/LV separation
V2: split HV and LV onto stacked boards joined by FFC, buffered SD card signals for reliability at speed, series resistor on the crystal for stability
V3: rigid-flex construction removing two connector failure points, full galvanic isolation, 40% smaller, ground-plane cutouts under switching regulators, BJT LED drivers protecting the GPIO

images.caption: V1: two-layer, M12 connectors, DPDT relay
V2: stacked boards, FFC link, full HV/LV split
V3 production board, 40% more compact than V2

sections.heading: Telemetry Board
bullets: 50Ω microstrip GPS antenna trace with load termination, impedance matched from module to connector to kill reflections
120Ω differential CAN with optocoupler isolation, placed away from switching supplies

images.caption: Telemetry board: impedance-matched GPS antenna trace and optocoupled CAN

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.content: Physically separating HV and LV beat any amount of clever layout on a shared board, and moving to rigid-flex removed an entire category of failure (connectors shaking loose) for a cost the vibration environment easily justified. Currently in assembly and enclosure design, with on-water testing next.

projects.title: Super Capacitor Power Module
projects.subtitle: Burst power assist for a high-agility competition robot
projects.description: Supercapacitor module that buffers peak current for a battle bot chassis. Built as captain of a team I co-founded.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: As captain and co-founder of Michigan Advanced Robotics Competition, I'm leading a supercapacitor module that sits between the battery and the drive system. It charges during low-demand phases and dumps current during hard acceleration and direction changes, keeping the robot responsive without hammering the battery.

sections.heading: The Challenge
bullets: Lithium packs sag under peak current, so the robot slows exactly when it shouldn't
Repeated high-current bursts across a full match, without thermal runaway or brownouts
Must fit the robot's weight and space budget and survive combat shock

sections.heading: Approach
bullets: Supercapacitor bank managed by a bidirectional DC-DC converter, gated on bus voltage and current demand
STM32 governs charge/discharge logic and drives MOSFETs for reverse-current blocking
Slow-start on the fused, regulated input to prevent inrush at high dV
Cell balancing keeps voltages even across the bank to prevent premature degradation

images.caption: V1 layout: fused regulated input, cap health monitor, regulated output

sections.heading: Status
sections.content: In active testing and development.

projects.title: Clarus
projects.subtitle: Routing for large vehicles built on measured LiDAR reality, not a restriction database
projects.description: 2nd place ($3,000) at the CYVL Hackathon. A 6-hour solo build that checks whether a fire truck can physically clear each turn, and reroutes when it can't.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Google Maps, Waze, and Route4Me route trucks off reported restriction databases, not measured road reality. Clarus routes off CYVL LiDAR data for Somerville, MA, checking each turn's swept path against real intersection geometry and obstacles like trees and utility poles, then rerouting around turns the vehicle physically cannot make. Built solo in six hours; 2nd of 12 teams.

sections.heading: Demo
sections.caption: Routing a fire truck through Somerville. The Large Vehicle profile flags a failing intersection and reroutes automatically.

sections.heading: The Challenge
bullets: Restriction databases carry wrong lane widths and missing turn restrictions, so GPS confidently sends a ladder truck into a corner it can't clear
No off-the-shelf tool checks a specific vehicle's swept path against a specific intersection's real geometry
Everything had to be derived: turning radii from AASHTO dimensions, road widths from centerlines, clearance from LiDAR asset positions

sections.heading: How It Works
bullets: Road graph: 1,535 nodes and 2,160 edges from CYVL centerlines, with 890 segments joined to PCI pavement scores
Turn check: computes the deviation angle and available radius at every intersection, compares against the vehicle's outer swing radius, returns pass / tight / fail with a plain-English reason
Three profiles on one Dijkstra core: Fastest (distance), Smoothest (PCI penalty, for ambulances), Large Vehicle (blocks failing intersections, then reroutes)
Swept path: via Autodesk APS, with a Shapely fallback that stays functional end-to-end so development never blocked on the API

images.caption: Three routing profiles compared live, with orange markers flagging tight or failing intersections

images.alt: Route segment with LiDAR clearance check
images.caption: Segment with 7.25 m measured overhead clearance
Point cloud of the Mystic Ave viaduct, where all four AASHTO design vehicles pass

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.content: Pavement condition and turn geometry are properties you have to measure, since they can't be crowd-sourced or inferred from map data. The turn feasibility math was the hardest part: correctly orienting entry and exit polyline vectors relative to the intersection node, where small direction bugs produced nonsensical angles.

projects.title: Next-Gen Industrial Gateway
projects.subtitle: Next-generation edge compute hardware for Laminar's sensors
projects.description: Compact IP67 enclosure for an off-the-shelf industrial PC, taken from CAD through CNC machining, assembly, and thermal validation.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Laminar's previous gateway ran on custom compute modules designed from scratch, but they were hard to manufacture and their performance didn't justify the cost. The company is switching to off-the-shelf (OTS) industrial PCs, and my task was to design a compact enclosure for them with good heat dissipation.

images.caption: V1: clear-lid enclosure with external heat sink

sections.heading: The Challenge
sections.content: These high-performance IPCs generate significant heat under load. They also sit directly on factory floors next to CIP lines, so the enclosure has to meet IP67:
bullets: Watertight: fully sealed to IP67
Heat dissipation: keeps the IPC cool under sustained load
Compact packaging: small, and laid out for easy assembly

images.caption: CNC-machined double-D keyholes for the Ethernet bulkhead connectors

sections.heading: Thermal Validation
sections.content: The graphs below compare the two versions. V2's aluminum enclosure and internal circulation fan ran significantly cooler, thanks to better internal convection, higher thermal mass, and higher thermal conductivity. Even over a run twice as long, V2 peaked 13 °C lower.

sections.heading: Results
sections.content: The V2 enclosure is now deployed at a real customer site.

images.alt: Team selfie at the customer site
images.caption: The team on deployment day

projects.title: LED Calibration Station
projects.subtitle: A calibration station that sweeps across light wavelengths to test Laminar's spectral sensors
projects.description: Modular LED calibration station for developing, testing, and validating Laminar's spectral sensors.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: One of several hardware projects I built during my summer 2026 internship at Laminar. The station calibrates Laminar's new Flex Sensor line, which fingerprints products to speed up CIP processes in CPG factories. It emits light across a range of wavelengths to simulate real-world emission spectra, so R&D can test sensors in-house and the contract manufacturer (CM) can validate units before they ship to customers.

sections.heading: The Challenge
sections.content: The requirements were open-ended, which left me free to define the station's form factor and capabilities. I prioritized three constraints:
bullets: Modularity: if Laminar ships sensors at new wavelengths, only a new LED breakout board is needed, not a full redesign
Flexible power input: runs off PoE, a barrel jack, or USB-C, with protection in case more than one source is connected at once
Ease of sensor change: the sensor under test mates to a socket on the main board, so units swap quickly in R&D or at the CM

sections.heading: Fixture & Bring-Up
sections.content: The fixture took a few attempts to get right. I wanted something users could snap on directly, with no changes to the sensor hardware. And as a personal challenge, it had to be satisfying to click into place.

images.caption: Main station with swappable breakout boards

sections.heading: Firmware
sections.content: I wrote all of the station's firmware, learning Zephyr RTOS from scratch along the way.
bullets: Work queue: calibration requests are queued and run in order without blocking the rest of the system
Interrupts: an ISR handles sensor swaps the moment they happen
Mutexes and semaphores: protect shared peripherals and keep threads in sync

images.caption: Solder jumpers to fix an I2C address conflict
A batch of boards off the bench
Debugging calibration board I2C traffic on the scope

projects.title: NIR Bulb Backup Circuit
projects.subtitle: An analog failover circuit for the bulb in Laminar's NIR sensors
projects.description: Analog failover bulb circuit that extends NIR sensor life in the field.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: I designed a failover circuit for the bulb in Laminar's NIR spectral sensor. The project landed on my desk in my second-to-last week, so the deadline was tight.

sections.heading: The Challenge
sections.content: One of my favorite projects at Laminar. The analog design was fun on its own, but the constraints made it even more interesting:
bullets: Fully analog: no digital signal can directly control the backup bulb, since the STM32H5 has no pins to spare
Small footprint: as small as possible, so the circuit can be integrated into different sensor packages as needed
Consistent performance: bulb one and bulb two have to perform the same

images.caption: Hand calculations for the comparator circuit
Simulating the backup bulb circuit in LTspice

sections.heading: Bench Validation
sections.content: Tolerance calculations let me spec shunt resistors that give a reliable switching threshold. I then mocked up the circuit on a breadboard using through-hole parts from the lab, and it worked.
